overview: This file documents the tightening Japanese control of foreign commercial activity in Dairen and the wider Manchurian market between 1934 and 1936. Its principal sequence concerns the Kwantung Army’s cancellation of a Japanese-American plan to assemble Chrysler vehicles in Dairen, apparently to protect an Army-controlled automobile enterprise in Manchukuo, followed by a compromise permitting limited hand assembly by the Fukusho Company. Later despatches report the establishment of a small Japanese-French engineering corporation associated with the South Manchuria Railway and the closure of a long-established British electrical-equipment office after discriminatory procurement practices and Japanese economic absorption deprived it of business. Together with a cross-reference sheet and an internal State Department appraisal, the documents illustrate military intervention, managed markets, foreign investment, and the displacement or accommodation of Western businesses in Japanese-controlled Northeast China.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch on Chrysler assembly plant
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to a related Manchuria file containing Vincent’s despatch about the proposed Chrysler assembly plant in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a 1934 Dairen despatch on establishing a Chrysler assembly plant, filed under 893.5034-Manchuria/3.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs appraisal of the Kwantung Army despatch
subfiles.about: An internal note recommends reading the Dairen despatch as evidence of Japanese military control over commerce in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Reviewer calls the despatch especially interesting, showing Japanese military authorities controlled even ordinary Manchurian commerce, recommending it be read in full.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Army blocks American automobile assembly plant in Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Vincent reports the Kwantung Army’s cancellation of permission for a Japanese-American company to assemble Chrysler automobiles in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Japanese and American commercial interests formed the Teikoku Jidosha Seisakusho to assemble Chrysler, Dodge, Plymouth, and De Soto vehicles for sale in Manchuria and China, after obtaining permits and investing in land, construction, and machinery. The Kwantung Army compelled the civil government to cancel the permit, ostensibly because the plant would compete with the Army-controlled Towa Jidosha Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha in Mukden. Vincent treats the case as evidence that the Army overruled resentful civil authorities and regarded Manchukuo and the Kwantung Leased Territory as a single economic unit. Although the American shareholders did not request diplomatic intervention, he argues that denying Chrysler the cost advantage of local assembly constituted an unreasonable restriction on American trade.

subfiles.title: Settlement of the Dairen automobile assembly dispute
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Vincent reports the apparent settlement of the dispute over the blocked automobile assembly company.
subfiles.summary: The plant site reverted to Fukusho, machinery passed to the Chrysler agent; the Army blocked a formal company but let Fukusho hand-assemble limited units, promising favorable future contract treatment to both Japanese and American participants.

subfiles.title: Formation of the Far Eastern Enterprise Corporation
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Grummon reports the organization, capitalization, objectives, and leadership of a Japanese-French engineering company in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Merlet and a Brossard, Mopin representative negotiated with the South Manchuria Railway to form the Far Eastern Enterprise Corporation, capitalized at 100,000 yen split between French and Railway-linked interests, for engineering and trading work.

subfiles.title: Closure of the General Electric Company of China office in Dairen
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Grummon presents the closure of a long-established British electrical firm’s Dairen office as evidence of the exclusion of foreign business from Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: General Electric Company of China closed its 17-year Dairen office as Japanese market domination eliminated opportunities; former manager Turner said bids were pointless given predetermined awards and plans solicited without real purchase intent.

interest: Shows three foreign-business outcomes under Kwantung Army pressure: constrained American, admitted French, and expelled British capital.
